# Which end of the fish would drop first?

**Short answer: the head end would drop first. The tail end would rise.**
The fish would tip head-down, pivoting in his remaining (right) hand — not
tail-down, which is the intuitive but incorrect expectation.

## What is in the picture

The foreground sailor (US Navy blue digital camouflage, black watch cap, safety
glasses, black work gloves) is carrying a large flat cut-out fish sign — a
plywood/board panel painted white and light blue with black outlines, now
smeared with tsunami mud — across a field of debris. A second sailor works
behind him with a blue tarp.

The fish is carried at a tilt:

- Its **head is low and to the viewer's left**: the painted eye, the gill line
  and the open, upturned mouth are at the far left of the frame, hanging out over
  a length of pipe and a heap of rubble.
- Its **tail is high and to the viewer's right**: the broad fan-shaped caudal fin
  is up against the sailor's chest/abdomen, with the narrow caudal peduncle just
  in front of it.
- Two rusty steel mounting brackets hang from the fish's bottom (belly) edge —
  this was a mounted sign.

## The two hands

- **The hand nearest the tail is his left hand.** It is up high on the right of
  the frame, gloved, hooked palm-down over the **top-rear corner of the tail
  fin** — effectively at the very tip of the fish (about 95% of the way back from
  the snout). His left forearm comes in roughly horizontally from his body, so
  that hand is draped over the corner rather than cupped under it.
- **The hand that stays is his right hand.** His right arm hangs down across the
  front of the panel and the gloved hand is **hooked under the fish's bottom
  (belly) edge, just behind the middle of the body** — behind the pectoral fin
  and behind the base of the tall dorsal fin, roughly 55–58% of the way back from
  the snout. The curled fingers reach below the belly edge, so the board's bottom
  edge rests in the crook of that fist. This is the hand actually carrying the
  weight.

## The mechanics

Once the left hand is gone, the fish is a rigid flat panel supported at
essentially **one point**: the right hand's hook grip under the belly edge. A
panel held at a single point below its centre of mass is unstable, so it will
rotate about that grip until its centre of mass swings beneath the support. The
only question is which way it rotates, and that is decided by which side of the
grip carries more weight.

Measuring the painted silhouette in the image (the fish spans about 1,200 pixels
from snout tip to tail tip):

- The **balance point of the cut-out is roughly 49% of the way back from the
  snout** — just behind the deepest part of the body, under the rear of the big
  dorsal fin. The head and body are bulky and deep; the tail fan is broad but the
  peduncle in front of it is narrow, and the whole tail fan is only about a fifth
  of the panel's area.
- The **remaining grip is behind that**, at roughly 55–58% of the length.
- So about 62% of the panel's area (and weight) lies on the head side of the
  remaining grip and only about 38% on the tail side. Taking moments about the
  grip, the head-side turning moment is roughly twice the tail-side moment.

Therefore the panel is **head-heavy about the hand that stays**, and on release
it tips **head-down / tail-up**: the head end swings down, the tail end kicks up
towards his chest.

This also explains the pose we actually see. Because the fish is head-heavy about
his right hand, his left hand is not holding the tail *up* — it is pressing the
raised tail corner *down* (a palm-down hook on the corner with a horizontal
forearm is well suited to pressing and steadying, and poorly suited to lifting).
It is the hand that stops the sign from nosing over, which is exactly the job
that is lost when he releases it. Consistently with that, the fish is already
sagging head-down in the photograph.

## Why the intuitive answer (the tail) is wrong here

The natural guess is that the released end is the end that falls. That would be
right if the remaining hand were forward of the balance point — i.e. nearer the
head, with the tail as the long unsupported overhang. It is not: his right hand
is at mid-body, and in fact it is *closer to the tail tip* (about 500 px) than to
the snout (about 690 px). The head-and-body side is the longer and much heavier
cantilever, so removing the tail-end support lets the *head* go down, with the
tail rising as the counterweight.

## What it would look like in practice

The head end is already the low end and is hanging only a few inches above the
horizontal pipe and rubble beneath it, so it would dip and strike that debris
almost immediately. The tail fin would rotate up and back against his chest. And
because his right hand is only a loose hook under a muddy edge, the likely real
outcome is that the sign slides out of that grip within the first fraction of a
turn and lands **head/nose first** on the debris.

## Stated caveat

The margin is modest — the remaining grip sits only about 8% of the fish's length
behind the balance point, so the fish is close to balanced in that hand and the
tip would be a gentle rotation rather than a violent swing. If his remaining hand
were in fact slightly forward of the balance point (nearer the head than
measured), the outcome would reverse and the tail would swing down instead. As
the hands are actually positioned in this photograph, however, the **head end
drops first and the tail end rises.**

Which end goes down depends on which side of the pivot holds more weight at a longer lever arm, not on which end was just released.

3. **The head end also reaches farther from the pivot.** The mouth is farther from the grip than the tail tip is, so the head's weight acts through a longer lever arm.

### 3. Center of Mass and Torque Analysis
* **Pivot Point:** If the man releases his left hand (the one holding the tail end) while keeping his right hand (on the left) in place, his right hand acts as the sole pivot/support point for the fish.
* **Distribution of Mass:**

  * The gravitational force acting on the right (tail) side has a much larger lever arm and mass, creating a powerful clockwise torque.
